concepts: Properties of determinants and polynomial coefficients
questions.question: If $\Delta=\left|\begin{matrix}x-2&2x-3&3x-4\\2x-3&3x-4&4x-5\\3x-5&5x-8&10x-17\end{matrix}\right|=Ax^3+Bx^2+Cx+D$, then $B+C$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Row and column operations remove most of the $x$ from the entries, so the cubic can be read off after one expansion.
solution: The three brackets are $-3x^2+6x$, $3x-8$ and $-1$, so $\Delta=-3x^3+12x^2-12x-3x+8-2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\Delta$ is a cubic, so $A$, $D$ and $A+B+C+D$ come from the leading coefficient, $\Delta(0)$ and $\Delta(1)$; then $B+C=\Delta(1)-A-D$.
solution: Put $x=1$: rows 1 and 2 both become $(-1,-1,-1)$, so $\Delta(1)=0$, i.e. $A+B+C+D=0$.
The $x^3$ coefficient is the determinant of the $x$-coefficients: $A=\left|\begin{matrix}1&2&3\\2&3&4\\3&5&10\end{matrix}\right|=10-16+3=-3$.

useful_results: For a determinant whose entries are linear in $x$, $\Delta(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $\le 3$: $\Delta(0)$ is the constant term, $\Delta(1)$ is the sum of all coefficients and the $x^3$ coefficient is the determinant of the matrix of $x$-coefficients.
Subtracting a multiple of one row (or column) from another does not change a determinant: use it to make entries constants, e.g. $R_2-2R_1$ turns a row of linear terms into $1,\,-x+2,\,-2x+3$.
Spot that two rows coincide at a special value of $x$ (here $x=1$) to get a coefficient sum without any expansion.

concepts: Homogeneous linear system: non-trivial integer solutions
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all integer solutions $(x,y,z)$ of the system $x-2y+5z=0$, $-2x+4y+z=0$, $-7x+14y+9z=0$ such that $15\le x^2+y^2+z^2\le150$. Then the number of elements in $S$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The coefficient determinant is $0$, so the solutions form a line; the first two equations give $z=0$, $x=2y$.
solution: The coefficient determinant is $D=1(36-14)+2(-18+7)+5(-28+28)=22-22+0=0$, so there are non-zero solutions.
Add $2\times$(first) to the second: $11z=0$, so $z=0$, and then $x=2k$.
Solutions: $(x,y,z)=(2k,k,0)$ with $k$ an integer (the third equation is satisfied automatically since $D=0$).
Hence the number of solutions is $8$.
questions.correction_note: Step 'Hence 1 <= k^2 <= 30' in the PDF should read 3 <= k^2 <= 30 (15 <= 5k^2 <= 150). With 1 <= k^2 the PDF's own list of k (5, 4, 3, 2) would also have to contain 1; the list and the count 8 are right, the printed inequality is wrong. The lower limit 15 is also garbled in the PDF text.

alternate_solutions.idea: Two independent equations give the solution line as the cross product of their coefficient vectors; the third equation is a combination of them.
solution: The third row is $R_3=R_1+4R_2$ (check: $1-8=-7$, $-2+16=14$, $5+4=9$), so it adds no new condition: the solution set is exactly the line $t(2,1,0)$.
Integer points: $(2k,k,0)$, $k\in\mathbb Z$ (as $(2,1,0)$ is a primitive vector), with $x^2+y^2+z^2=5k^2$.
$15\le5k^2\le150\Rightarrow3\le k^2\le30\Rightarrow|k|\in\{2,3,4,5\}$, i.e. $8$ values of $k$. Same answer.

useful_results: If the rank of a $3\times3$ homogeneous system is $2$, the solution set is the line through the origin along the cross product of any two independent rows.
If a row is a combination of the others, e.g. $R_3=R_1+4R_2$ here, it carries no new information; finding that combination proves $D=0$ without expanding.

Lattice points on the line $\mathbb{R}\,\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v}$ a primitive integer vector are exactly $k\mathbf{v}$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, and $|k\mathbf v|^2=k^2|\mathbf v|^2$; count the $k$ with $m\le k^2|\mathbf v|^2\le M$ and remember the negative $k$.

questions.question: If the minimum and the maximum values of the function $f:\left[\frac\pi4,\frac\pi2\right]\to\mathbb R$, defined by $f(\theta)=\left|\begin{matrix}-\sin^2\theta&-1-\sin^2\theta&1\\-\cos^2\theta&-1-\cos^2\theta&1\\12&10&-2\end{matrix}\right|$ are $m$ and $M$ respectively, then the ordered pair $(m,M)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $C_2\to C_2-C_1+C_3$ kills the $\theta$-terms in the second column and leaves $4\cos2\theta$.
solution: Apply $C_2\to C_2-C_1+C_3$: the entries of the new column are $-1-\sin^2\theta+\sin^2\theta+1=0$, $-1-\cos^2\theta+\cos^2\theta+1=0$ and $10-12-2=-4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ through $R_1-R_2$, which gives a row proportional to $(1,1,0)$ and factors out $\cos2\theta$.
solution: So $f=4\cos2\theta$, and on $\left[\frac\pi4,\frac\pi2\right]$ it ranges over $[-4,0]$: option (D). Same answer.

useful_results: When entries contain both $\sin^2\theta$ and $\cos^2\theta$, a row or column difference like $R_1-R_2$ turns them into $\cos2\theta$ and a common factor comes out of the row.
$\cos2\theta=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta$ decreases from $0$ to $-1$ as $\theta$ goes from $\frac\pi4$ to $\frac\pi2$ (use the interval of $2\theta$, not of $\theta$).
If a determinant has the form $|u,\;u\!-\!w\!+\!\text{const}\!\cdot\! e,\;w|$, then $C_2\to C_2-C_1+C_3$ cancels the $\theta$-dependent parts: look for such a combination of columns first.

concepts: Properties of determinants (row and column operations)
questions.question: If $a+x=b+y=c+z+1$, where $a,b,c,x,y,z$ are non-zero distinct real numbers, then $\left|\begin{matrix}x&a+y&x+a\\y&b+y&y+b\\z&c+y&z+c\end{matrix}\right|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Column operations make the second column $(y,y,y)$ so $y$ factors out; the two given equalities then fix $x-y$ and $y-z$.
solution: Apply $C_3\to C_3-C_1$: the third column becomes $(a,b,c)$, so $\Delta=\left|\begin{matrix}x&a+y&a\\y&b+y&b\\z&c+y&c\end{matrix}\right|$.
Apply $C_2\to C_2-C_3$: the second column becomes $(y,y,y)$, so $\Delta=\left|\begin{matrix}x&y&a\\y&y&b\\z&y&c\end{matrix}\right|$.
Expand along the second column (the only non-zero entry is $1$ in position $(3,2)$, sign $-$): $\Delta=-y\left[(x-y)(b-c)-(y-z)(a-b)\right]$.
questions.correction_note: Two slips in the PDF: (1) after C2->C2-C3 the first entry of the second column is printed as x; it should be y (otherwise y cannot be taken out of C2). (2) In the last line the factor is printed (c-b-1); since y-z = c-b+1 (from b+y=c+z+1) it must be (c-b+1). With (c-b-1) the printed expression would give y(b-a), not the stated y(a-b). Final answer (C) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: The result is an identity, so test the options with one admissible set of numbers.
solution: Take $a=1$, $b=2$, $c=5$, $y=3$; then $a+x=b+y=5$ gives $x=4$ and $c+z+1=5$ gives $z=-1$. All six numbers $1,2,5,4,3,-1$ are non-zero and distinct.
The options give: $0$; $y(b-a)=3$; $y(a-b)=-3$; $y(a-c)=-12$. Only $y(a-b)=-3$ matches: option (C). Same answer.

useful_results: Adding a multiple of one column to another leaves a determinant unchanged; use it to create repeated entries such as $(y,y,y)$ and then factor the common value out.
A constraint like $a+x=b+y$ is best used at the end, to replace differences such as $x-y$ by $b-a$.

For an identity-type MCQ, substituting one admissible numerical set and checking the options (here $-3$) is a fast, reliable check; make sure the chosen numbers satisfy every condition of the question.

concepts: Homogeneous linear system with non-zero solution (determinant = 0)
questions.question: If the system of linear equations $x+y+3z=0$, $x+3y+k^2z=0$, $3x+y+3z=0$ has a non-zero solution $(x,y,z)$ for some $k\in\mathbb R$, then $x+\frac yz$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A non-zero solution needs $D=0$, which fixes $k^2=9$; subtracting two equations then gives $x=0$ and $y/z$.
solution: Then (1) gives $y+3z=0$, so $\frac yz=-3$ (and (2) is satisfied).

alternate_solutions.idea: Equations 1 and 3 do not contain $k$; subtracting them gives $x=0$ at once, and $y/z$ follows without finding $k$.
solution: If $z=0$ then $y=0$ and the solution is trivial; a non-zero solution therefore has $z\ne0$ and $\frac yz=-3$.
(Consistency: equation 2 becomes $3y+k^2z=-9z+k^2z=0$, which holds for $z\ne0$ exactly when $k^2=9$, so such a $k$ exists.)

useful_results: Before computing $D$, look for two equations that do not contain the parameter: combining them can fix the unknowns without finding the parameter.
A homogeneous system always has the zero solution; non-zero solutions exist iff $D=0$ (rank $<$ number of unknowns), and then only ratios such as $y/z$ are determined.
When asked for a ratio $y:z$ at the end, always check that the denominator ($z$) cannot be zero for a non-trivial solution.

questions.question: Let $m$ and $M$ be respectively the minimum and maximum values of $\left|\begin{matrix}\cos^2x&1+\sin^2x&\sin2x\\1+\cos^2x&\sin^2x&\sin2x\\\cos^2x&\sin^2x&1+\sin2x\end{matrix}\right|$. Then the ordered pair $(m,M)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $R_2-R_1$ and $R_3-R_1$ create two rows of constants, leaving $-2-\sin2x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $R_1-R_3$ and $R_2-R_3$ instead: the first two rows become the constant rows $(0,1,-1)$ and $(1,0,-1)$.

useful_results: Differences of rows that share most entries reduce a determinant to a few unit entries; try the differences with every row and keep the pair that gives the most constants.
For a determinant of the form $a\pm\sin2x$ (or $\sin x\cos x$), the extreme values come from $\sin2x=\pm1$; the range of $p+q\sin\phi$ is $[p-|q|,p+|q|]$.
Always finish by checking that the extremes are really attained in the allowed domain (here $x$ is unrestricted, so both are attained).

concepts: Homogeneous linear system: non-zero solutions and determinant
questions.question: The sum of distinct values of $\lambda$ for which the system of equations $(\lambda-1)x+(3\lambda+1)y+2\lambda z=0$, $(\lambda-1)x+(4\lambda-2)y+(\lambda+3)z=0$, $2x+(3\lambda+1)y+3(\lambda-1)z=0$ has non-zero solutions, is ______.
questions.key_idea: Non-zero solutions need $D=0$; $R_1-R_2$ has the common factor $\lambda-3$, which splits the work.
solution: Apply $R_1\to R_1-R_2$: the first row becomes $(0,\,-\lambda+3,\,\lambda-3)$.
So $\lambda=3$ or the remaining determinant is $0$. Apply $C_2\to C_2+C_3$: $\left|\begin{matrix}0&0&1\\\lambda-1&5\lambda+1&\lambda+3\\2&6\lambda-2&3\lambda-3\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
The distinct values are $0$ and $3$, so the sum is $0+3=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat it as a system: $R_1-R_2$ forces $y=z$ unless $\lambda=3$, which reduces the problem to a $2\times2$ determinant.
solution: Case $\lambda=3$: equations 1 and 2 become identical, $2x+10y+6z=0$, so the rank is at most $2$ and non-zero solutions exist. So $\lambda=3$ works.
These have a non-zero $(x,y)$ iff $(\lambda-1)(6\lambda-2)-2(5\lambda+1)=6\lambda^2-18\lambda=0$, i.e. $\lambda=0$ (since $\lambda\ne3$ here).
Check $\lambda=0$: $y=z$ and $-x+y=0$ gives $(1,1,1)$, which satisfies all three equations. The distinct values are $0,3$, sum $=3$. Same answer.

useful_results: If two rows of a coefficient matrix differ by a multiple of a vector with a parameter factor, e.g. $R_1-R_2=(\lambda-3)(0,-1,1)$, then $(\lambda-3)$ divides $D$, and $D$ vanishes at that value for the trivial reason that two rows coincide.
The sum of distinct roots asked for is cleaner by factorisation: here $D=6\lambda(\lambda-3)^2$, so the distinct roots are $0,3$ (do not add the repeated root twice).
For a system with a parameter, split into the case that makes a row combination vanish and the generic case, and check the special values directly.

concepts: Consistency of linear systems: unique, no and infinitely many solutions
questions.question:
For the system of linear equations $x-2y=1$, $x-y+kz=-2$, $ky+4z=6$, $k\in\mathbb R$, consider the statements: (A) The system has a unique solution if $k
e2,\,k
e-2$. (B) The system has a unique solution if $k=-2$. (C) The system has a unique solution if $k=2$. (D) The system has no solution if $k=2$. (E) The system has infinitely many solutions if $k
e-2$. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.key_idea: $D=4-k^2$ separates the unique case from the special values $k=\pm2$, and $D_x\ne0$ at $k=2$ shows there is no solution.
solution: If $D\ne0$, i.e. $k\ne\pm2$, the system has a unique solution, so (A) is true.
Statements (B), (C) and (E) are false: for $k=\pm2$ the determinant $D=0$ so the solution is not unique, and for $k\ne\pm2$ the solution is unique (not infinite), so (E) is false.
If $k=2$: $D=0$ and $D_x=-(12)(4)\ne0$, so the system has no solution; (D) is true.
(At $k=-2$: $D=D_x=0$ and the system has infinitely many solutions, which also shows (B) is false.)
Hence (A) and (D) are the true statements: option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $x$ from the first two equations to get a $2\times2$ system in $y,z$ and read off the three cases directly.
solution: From the first equation $x=1+2y$. Substituting into the second: $1+2y-y+kz=-2$, i.e. $y+kz=-3$.
With the third equation we have $y+kz=-3$ and $ky+4z=6$, with coefficient determinant $4-k^2$.
If $k\ne\pm2$ this is non-zero: unique $(y,z)$ and hence a unique $x$. So (A) is true.
$k=2$: $y+2z=-3$ and $2y+4z=6$; the second is $y+2z=3$, contradicting the first, so no solution: (D) is true.
$k=-2$: $y-2z=-3$ and $-2y+4z=6$ are the same equation, so infinitely many solutions. Thus (B) and (C) are false, and (E) is false (for $k\ne-2$ the solution is not infinite).
True statements: (A) and (D), option (D). Same answer.

useful_results: A $3\times3$ system has a unique solution iff $D\ne0$; if $D=0$ look at $D_x,D_y,D_z$ or reduce the augmented matrix: all $D$'s zero does not by itself prove infinitely many solutions, check the rank.
At the special values the system may have no solution at one value ($k=2$) and infinitely many at the other ($k=-2$): test each value separately.
For statements involving a parameter, elimination of one variable gives a smaller system in which the cases show up as a single factor such as $4-k^2$.

concepts: Unique solution of a linear system (determinant test)
questions.question: The following system of linear equations $2x+3y+2z=9$, $3x+2y+2z=9$, $x-y+4z=8$: (A) Has infinitely many solutions (B) Has a solution $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ satisfying $\alpha+\beta^2+\gamma^2=12$ (C) Does not have any solution (D) Has a unique solution
questions.key_idea: A non-zero coefficient determinant means exactly one solution, which rules out (A), (B)'s extra solution and (C).
solution: Since $\Delta\ne0$, the system has a unique solution: option (D).
(Solving gives $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(1,1,2)$ with $\alpha+\beta^2+\gamma^2=1+1+4=6\ne12$, so (B) is also false.)
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes 2(8+2) - 3(12-2) + 2(-3-2) = 32 - 30 - 10 = -8. The first term is 2*10 = 20, not 32, so the determinant is 20 - 30 - 10 = -20 (checked by computer). It is non-zero either way, so the conclusion (D) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve by elimination: subtracting the first two equations gives $x=y$ and the solution drops out.
solution: Eq.1 becomes $5x+2z=9$ and Eq.3 becomes $x-x+4z=8$, so $z=2$.
Then $5x=5$, $x=1$, $y=1$: the unique solution is $(1,1,2)$ (check Eq.2: $3+2+4=9$).
For this solution $\alpha+\beta^2+\gamma^2=1+1+4=6\ne12$, so (B) fails; the solution is unique, so (D). Same answer.

useful_results: Unique solution of $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ (square $A$) $\iff\det A\ne0$; the right-hand side does not matter.
When asked only whether a solution exists and is unique, evaluate $\det A$ and stop; for statements that quote a particular solution, find the solution too.
Quick check of a $3\times3$ determinant: expand along a row with small entries and recompute with a different row.

concepts: Consistency of linear systems: infinitely many solutions (Cramer's rule)
questions.question: Consider the system $x+2y-3z=a$, $2x+6y-11z=b$, $x-2y+7z=c$, where $a,b,c$ are real constants. Then the system of equations: (A) has no solution for all $a,b,c$ (B) has infinite number of solutions when $5a=2b+c$ (C) has a unique solution when $5a=2b+c$ (D) has a unique solution for all $a,b,c$
options: has infinite number of solutions when $5a=2b+c$
has a unique solution for all $a,b,c$
questions.answer: (B) has infinite number of solutions when $5a=2b+c$
questions.key_idea: $D=0$ rules out (D); the three numerators share the factor $5a-2b-c$, so they vanish together exactly when $5a=2b+c$.
solution: If $5a-2b-c=0$ then $D=D_x=D_y=D_z=0$ and the system has infinitely many solutions (it is consistent, since the rank of the coefficient matrix is $2$).
If $5a-2b-c\ne0$ then $D=0$ but $D_x\ne0$: no solution. So the system never has a unique solution.
Hence the system has infinitely many solutions exactly when $5a=2b+c$: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Gaussian elimination: the third row reduces to $0=c+2b-5a$, the consistency condition.
solution: The system is consistent iff $5a=2b+c$; then only two independent equations remain in three unknowns, so $z$ is free: infinitely many solutions.
If $5a\ne2b+c$ there is no solution; a unique solution never occurs. Hence (B). Same answer.

useful_results: For a singular matrix $A$, $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is consistent iff $\mathbf b$ is orthogonal to the null vector of $A^{T}$: here $(-5,2,1)A=\mathbf0$ gives $-5a+2b+c=0$.
If $D=0$ and some $D_x\ne0$ the system has no solution; if $D=D_x=D_y=D_z=0$ it is NOT automatic that it has infinitely many (rank may be $1$ with inconsistency): confirm by row reduction.
The numerators $D_x,D_y,D_z$ are all multiples of the same consistency expression $5a-2b-c$ here, a sign that the rows are dependent.

concepts: Homogeneous linear system and circulant-type determinant
Relations between roots and coefficients of a cubic
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the real roots of the equation $x^3+ax^2+bx+c=0$ ($a,b,c\in\mathbb R$ and $a,b\ne0$). If the system of equations (in $u,v,w$) given by $\alpha u+\beta v+\gamma w=0$; $\beta u+\gamma v+\alpha w=0$; $\gamma u+\alpha v+\beta w=0$ has a non-trivial solution, then the value of $\frac{a^2}{b}$ is:
questions.key_idea: The determinant is the circulant $-(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3-3\alpha\beta\gamma)$, which vanishes only if $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$ or $\alpha=\beta=\gamma$.
solution: But $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-a$ and $a\ne0$, so $\alpha+\beta+\gamma\ne0$. Hence $\alpha=\beta=\gamma$ (the roots are real, so each square must be $0$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Express the circulant determinant through Vieta's relations: it equals $a(a^2-3b)$, so $a\ne0$ forces $a^2=3b$ directly.
solution: A non-trivial solution needs $\det=0$; since $a\ne0$, $a^2=3b$, and $b\ne0$ gives $\frac{a^2}{b}=3$: option (B). Same answer.

useful_results: The circulant determinant $\left|\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha&\beta&\gamma\\\beta&\gamma&\alpha\\\gamma&\alpha&\beta\end{smallmatrix}\right|=-(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3-3\alpha\beta\gamma)=-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2-\alpha\beta-\beta\gamma-\gamma\alpha)$ is zero iff $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$ or $\alpha=\beta=\gamma$ (for real numbers).

For a cubic $x^3+ax^2+bx+c$ with roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$: $\sum\alpha=-a$, $\sum\alpha\beta=b$, so $\sum\alpha^2-\sum\alpha\beta=a^2-3b$, and $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3-3\alpha\beta\gamma=-a(a^2-3b)$.
The Vieta route works even for non-real roots, while 'all equal' needs the roots to be real: when $a^2=3b$ the cubic need not be a perfect cube, so $c$ is not forced.

concepts: Unique and infinitely many solutions of a linear system
questions.question: Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be respectively the sets of all $a\in\mathbb R-\{0\}$ for which the system of linear equations $ax+2ay-3az=1$, $(2a+1)x+(2a+3)y+(a+1)z=2$, $(3a+5)x+(a+5)y+(a+2)z=3$ has a unique solution and infinitely many solutions. Then:
questions.key_idea: $D=a\,(15a^2+31a+37)$ and the quadratic factor has negative discriminant, so $D\ne0$ for every $a\ne0$.
solution: A unique solution needs $D\ne0$; infinitely many solutions need $D=0$ (and consistency).
$D=\left|\begin{matrix}a&2a&-3a\\2a+1&2a+3&a+1\\3a+5&a+5&a+2\end{matrix}\right|$; take $a$ out of $R_1$ and clear the first column with $R_2-(2a+1)R_1'$, $R_3-(3a+5)R_1'$.
The new second and third rows are $(0,\,1-2a,\,7a+4)$ and $(0,\,-5a-5,\,10a+17)$.
The quadratic $15a^2+31a+37$ has discriminant $31^2-4\cdot15\cdot37=961-2220=-1259<0$ and positive leading coefficient, so it is positive for all real $a$.
Hence $D\ne0$ for all $a\in\mathbb R-\{0\}$: the system has a unique solution for every such $a$.
questions.correction_note: The coefficient matrix printed in the PDF has 2a+1 in the third entry of the second row, but the equation (and the printed value D = a(15a^2+31a+37)) uses a+1; with 2a+1 the determinant would be a(20a^2+36a+37). The matrix entry is corrected to a+1. The PDF also gives no working for D and for the sign of the quadratic; both are added. The answer (B) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: The first row sums to $0$, so adding the other two columns into the third column puts a zero at the top.
solution: $C_3\to C_3+C_1+C_2$: the third column becomes $(0,\;5a+5,\;5a+12)^T$; the determinant is unchanged.
So $D\ne0$ for $a\ne0$: unique solution always, $S_1=\mathbb R-\{0\}$, $S_2=\phi$: option (B). Same answer.

useful_results: A column (or row) sum trick: if the entries of one row add up to $0$, replace a column by the sum of all columns to create a zero entry before expanding.
A quadratic $pa^2+qa+r$ with $p>0$ and $q^2-4pr<0$ is positive for all real $a$; use this to show a determinant never vanishes.
For $n(S)$-type options, decide first whether the determinant can vanish at all: if $D\ne0$ for all admissible parameter values, then the set for 'infinitely many solutions' is empty.

questions.question: If $1$, $\log_{10}(4^x-2)$ and $\log_{10}\left(4^x+\frac{18}5\right)$ are in arithmetic progression for a real number $x$, then the value of the determinant $\left|\begin{matrix}2\left(x-\frac12\right)&x-1&x^2\\1&0&x\\x&1&0\end{matrix}\right|$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The A.P. condition gives $(4^x-2)^2=10\cdot4^x+36$, a quadratic in $4^x$ whose admissible root is $16$, so $x=2$.
solution: Since the terms are in A.P., $2\log_{10}\left(4^x-2\right)=1+\log_{10}\left(4^x+\frac{18}5\right)$.
At $x=2$ the entries are $2\left(2-\tfrac12\right)=3$, $x-1=1$, $x^2=4$: the determinant is $\left|\begin{matrix}3&1&4\\1&0&2\\2&1&0\end{matrix}\right|$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand the determinant symbolically first: it factorises as $x(x-1)^2$, so the answer is read off at $x=2$ without a numerical $3\times3$ expansion.
solution: Expand along the first row: $(2x-1)(0\cdot0-x\cdot1)-(x-1)(1\cdot0-x\cdot x)+x^2(1\cdot1-0\cdot x)$.
The A.P. condition again gives $y=4^x=16$, hence $x=2$ (the root $y=-2$ is rejected as $4^x>0$).

useful_results: Three numbers $p,q,r$ are in A.P. iff $2q=p+r$; with logarithms $2\log_{10}u=1+\log_{10}v$ becomes $u^2=10v$ (and $u,v>0$ must hold).
An equation in $4^x$ (or $a^x$) becomes a quadratic in $y=a^x$; always reject the roots with $y\le0$ and also those making the log arguments non-positive.
If a determinant has entries polynomial in $x$ and you must evaluate it at one value of $x$, either evaluate directly or expand symbolically; checking both ways guards against arithmetic slips.

questions.question: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&b&1\\b&b^2+1&b\\1&b&2\end{bmatrix}$ where $b>0$. Then the minimum value of $\frac{\det(A)}{b}$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\det A=b^2+3$, so $\frac{\det A}b=b+\frac3b$ and AM-GM gives the minimum.
solution: So $b+\frac3b\ge2\sqrt3$, with equality at $b=\sqrt3$. The minimum is $2\sqrt3$: option (D).
$f(b)=\frac{\det A}{b}=b+\frac3b$, $f'(b)=1-\frac3{b^2}=0\Rightarrow b=\sqrt3$ ($b>0$); $f''(b)=\frac6{b^3}>0$, so it is a minimum.

useful_results: Matrix determinant lemma: $\det(I+uv^T)=1+v^Tu$; for $A=I+vv^T$ the determinant is $1+|v|^2$. Recognise a matrix as 'identity plus a rank-one matrix' whenever off-diagonal entries are products $v_iv_j$.
For $t>0$ and $k>0$: $t+\frac kt\ge2\sqrt k$ with equality at $t=\sqrt k$; here $k=3$.
AM-GM needs the terms to be positive and the product to be a constant; check both before using it (here $b>0$ and $b\cdot\frac3b=3$).

concepts: Maximum and minimum values of trigonometric expressions
questions.question: If $d\in\mathbb R$ and $A=\begin{bmatrix}-2&4+d&(\sin\theta)-2\\1&(\sin\theta)+2&d\\5&(2\sin\theta)-d&(-\sin\theta)+2+2d\end{bmatrix}$, $\theta\in[0,2\pi]$. If the minimum value of $\det(A)$ is $8$, then a value of $d$ is:
questions.key_idea: $R_1+R_3-2R_2=(1,0,0)$, which collapses the determinant to $(d+2)^2-\sin^2\theta$.
solution: Apply $R_1\to R_1+R_3-2R_2$: the first entry is $-2+5-2=1$, the second $(4+d)+(2\sin\theta-d)-2(\sin\theta+2)=0$, the third $(\sin\theta-2)+(-\sin\theta+2+2d)-2d=0$.
Only $d=-5$ appears among the options: option (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's expansion line 'A(theta) = (sin t + 2)(2 + 2d - sin t) - sin t + 2 + 2d' is not a correct expansion: the (sin t + 2)(2 + 2d - sin t) term must be followed by -d(2 sin t - d), and the printed tail '- sin t + 2 + 2d' does not occur. The correct expansion is given (it equals (d+2)^2 - sin^2 t, which is what the PDF states next). The values d = 1, -5 and the answer (B) are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\det A$ is a quadratic in $s=\sin\theta$; split the two $s$-dependent columns and use multilinearity, then read the coefficients.
solution: $d+2=\pm3$, $d=1$ or $-5$; only $-5$ is listed: option (B). Same answer.

useful_results: If every entry of a determinant is linear in a variable $s$, the determinant is a polynomial of degree at most the number of $s$-dependent columns (or rows); its coefficients can be found column by column by multilinearity.
To minimise $g-\sin^2\theta$ over all $\theta$ use $\sin^2\theta\in[0,1]$: minimum $g-1$ at $\sin^2\theta=1$, maximum $g$ at $\sin^2\theta=0$.
A quadratic equation for the parameter usually gives two values ($d=1$ and $d=-5$); the options decide which one is asked for.
Look for a combination of rows such as $R_1+R_3-2R_2$ that produces a unit vector: the entries are often built so that a second difference cancels.

questions.question: Let $P=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\3&1&0\\9&3&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $Q=[q_{ij}]$ be two $3\times3$ matrices such that $Q-P^5=I_3$. Then $\frac{q_{21}+q_{31}}{q_{32}}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Compute $P^2,P^3,\dots,P^5$ (the pattern is regular) and use $Q=I_3+P^5$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the (3,1) entry of P^2 as 9 + 3x3 + 1, which equals 19; the correct value is 9 + 3x3 + 9 = 27 (row (9,3,1) times column (1,3,9)). It then jumps to P^5 without showing P^3, P^4; P^5 = [[1,0,0],[15,1,0],[135,15,1]] as printed is correct (checked by computer), so the answer 10 is unchanged. P^3 and P^4 are added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $P=I+N$ with $N$ nilpotent ($N^3=0$) and use the binomial theorem.

useful_results: For $P=I+N$ with $N^k=O$: $P^n=\sum_{j<k}\binom njN^j$; here $P^n=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\3n&1&0\\\frac{9n(n+1)}{2}&3n&1\end{bmatrix}$ (check $n=5$: $135,15$).
Strictly triangular matrices are nilpotent: an $m\times m$ strictly lower-triangular $N$ satisfies $N^m=O$.
A lower-triangular matrix with $1$s on the diagonal has determinant $1$; its powers keep the shape and the first subdiagonal grows like $n$.

questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}e^t&e^{-t}\cos t&e^{-t}\sin t\\e^t&-e^{-t}\cos t-e^{-t}\sin t&-e^{-t}\sin t+e^{-t}\cos t\\e^t&2e^{-t}\sin t&-2e^{-t}\cos t\end{bmatrix}$, then $A$ is:
questions.key_idea: Pull $e^{t}$, $e^{-t}$, $e^{-t}$ out of the three columns; the remaining determinant turns out to be the constant $5$.
solution: Take $e^t$ out of $C_1$ and $e^{-t}$ out of each of $C_2,C_3$: $|A|=e^{-t}\left|\begin{matrix}1&\cos t&\sin t\\1&-\cos t-\sin t&-\sin t+\cos t\\1&2\sin t&-2\cos t\end{matrix}\right|$.
Apply $R_2\to R_2-R_1$, $R_3\to R_3-R_1$: $|A|=e^{-t}\left|\begin{matrix}1&\cos t&\sin t\\0&-2\cos t-\sin t&-2\sin t+\cos t\\0&2\sin t-\cos t&-2\cos t-\sin t\end{matrix}\right|$.
Expand along the first column: $|A|=e^{-t}\left[(2\cos t+\sin t)^2+(2\sin t-\cos t)^2\right]$.
$(2\cos t+\sin t)^2+(2\sin t-\cos t)^2=4\cos^2t+4\sin t\cos t+\sin^2t+4\sin^2t-4\sin t\cos t+\cos^2t=5$.
Hence $A$ is invertible for all $t\in\mathbb R$: option (C).
questions.correction_note: Two slips in the PDF: (1) after R2->R2-R1 the second entry of row 2 is printed as -cos t - sin t; it should be -2cos t - sin t (the value used afterwards, (2cos t + sin t)^2, needs it). (2) The factor e^{-t} (from the columns) is dropped: the PDF ends with |A| = 5, the correct value is |A| = 5e^{-t} (checked by computer). Both do not change the answer (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: The three rows are $f,f',f''$ of three functions, so $\det A$ is a Wronskian and Abel's identity gives $W(t)=W(0)e^{-t}$.
solution: Let $f_1=e^t$, $f_2=e^{-t}\cos t$, $f_3=e^{-t}\sin t$. Differentiating the first row gives the second row, and differentiating the second gives the third (e.g. $f_3''=-2e^{-t}\cos t$).
These are solutions of the equation with characteristic roots $1,\,-1\pm i$: $(r-1)(r^2+2r+2)=r^3+r^2-2$, i.e. $y'''+y''-2y=0$.
$\det A=5e^{-t}\ne0$ for all $t$: option (C). Same answer.

useful_results: A square matrix is invertible iff its determinant is non-zero; for functions of $t$ check whether the determinant is a non-zero constant times a never-vanishing factor like $e^{-t}$.
Wronskian of $y'''+py''+qy'+ry=0$: $W(t)=W(0)\,e^{-pt}$, so a fundamental set of solutions has a Wronskian that never vanishes.
A column pattern $(f,f',f'')^T$ with $f=e^{\lambda t},\,e^{-t}\cos t,\,e^{-t}\sin t$ is a signal to think Wronskian.

questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha\\\sin\alpha&\cos\alpha\end{pmatrix}$, $(\alpha\in\mathbb R)$ such that $A^{32}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, then a value of $\alpha$ is:
questions.key_idea: $A^n$ is the rotation through $n\alpha$, so $A^{32}$ has $\cos32\alpha=0$ and $\sin32\alpha=1$.
solution: Continuing, $A^{16}$ is the rotation with $16\alpha$ and $A^{32}=A^{16}A^{16}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos32\alpha&-\sin32\alpha\\\sin32\alpha&\cos32\alpha\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Identify the matrix with the complex number $e^{i\alpha}$: powers become $e^{in\alpha}$ and the target matrix is $i$.
solution: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha\\\sin\alpha&\cos\alpha\end{pmatrix}$ represents multiplication by $e^{i\alpha}$ on $x+iy$, and the map $z\mapsto$ matrix respects products.
Test the options: $\frac\pi{32}$ gives $e^{i\pi}=-1$, $0$ gives $1$, $\frac\pi{16}$ gives $e^{2\pi i}=1$; only $\frac\pi{64}$ gives $i$: option (B). Same answer.

useful_results: $R(\alpha)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha\\\sin\alpha&\cos\alpha\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $R(\alpha)R(\beta)=R(\alpha+\beta)$ and $R(\alpha)^n=R(n\alpha)$ for all integers $n$.
$R(\alpha)\leftrightarrow e^{i\alpha}$: matrix identities become complex-number identities.
$R(\pi/2)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $R(\pi)=-I$, $R(2\pi)=I$: the order of $R(\alpha)$ is the smallest $n$ with $n\alpha\in2\pi\mathbb Z$.

questions.question: Let the numbers $2,b,c$ be in an A.P. and $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\2&b&c\\4&b^2&c^2\end{bmatrix}$. If $\det(A)\in[2,16]$, then $c$ lies in the interval:
questions.key_idea: $\det A$ is a Vandermonde determinant; with common difference $d$ it equals $2d^3$.
solution: Since $2,b,c$ are in A.P. with common difference $d$: $b-2=c-b=d$ and $c-2=2d$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The determinant is the Vandermonde determinant of the numbers $2,b,c$; quote its product formula.
solution: Rows $(1,1,1)$, $(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, $(x_1^2,x_2^2,x_3^2)$ with $(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(2,b,c)$ give the Vandermonde determinant $\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)=(b-2)(c-2)(c-b)$.
For an A.P. $2,\,2+d,\,2+2d$ the three differences are $d,\,2d,\,d$, so $\det A=2d^3$.

useful_results: Vandermonde: $\left|\begin{smallmatrix}1&1&1\\x&y&z\\x^2&y^2&z^2\end{smallmatrix}\right|=(y-x)(z-x)(z-y)$; it vanishes iff two of the numbers coincide.
For numbers in A.P. with common difference $d$ the Vandermonde determinant is $2d^3$ (differences $d,2d,d$), so its sign is the sign of $d$.
The map $d\mapsto2d^3$ is increasing, so an interval condition on the determinant translates to an interval condition on $d$ by taking cube roots.

concepts: Product and inverse of unipotent matrices
Sum of first n natural numbers
questions.question: If $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\cdot\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\cdot\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\cdots\begin{bmatrix}1&n-1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&78\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, then the inverse of $\begin{bmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\begin{bmatrix}1&p\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&q\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&p+q\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, so the product adds the upper-right entries.
solution: Since $\begin{bmatrix}1&p\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&q\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&p+q\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, the product of the matrices is $\begin{bmatrix}1&1+2+3+\cdots+(n-1)\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$.

The inverse of $\begin{bmatrix}1&13\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ is $\begin{bmatrix}1&-13\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, since $\begin{bmatrix}1&13\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&-13\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$: option (B).
useful_results: The matrices $U(p)=\begin{bmatrix}1&p\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ satisfy $U(p)U(q)=U(p+q)$, so $U(p)^{-1}=U(-p)$ and $U(p)^n=U(np)$; they commute with each other.
$1+2+\cdots+m=\frac{m(m+1)}2$; $78=\frac{12\cdot13}2$, so $\frac{(n-1)n}2=78$ is solved by $n-1=12$, i.e. $n=13$ (check by $n(n-1)=156=13\cdot12$).
Same idea for lower-triangular $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\p&1\end{bmatrix}$: they also add their off-diagonal entries.
